reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes free or rapid BNB through a flash-loan arbitrage bot and presents the result as easy and tested. It directs viewers to copy contract code, connect MetaMask, enter a large loan amount, and send BNB to the contract, including an additional transfer if the first payment does not work. The demonstration includes a wallet-connected contract workflow and a recorded BNB outflow, although the recipient, contract behavior, actual profit, and any completed loss are not established.

citations.quote: Flashloan Arbitrage bot for FREE BNB (UPDATED-Feb 2022) Easy trick 100% Tested!
Earn free bnb using flashloan arbitrage techniques GO TO - Remix Link
COPY EXACT CODE
Change the environment to (injected Web3) and Connect your wallet when prompted (Metamask Preferable)
Enter your token details and deploy the contract (you can enter any name) and Enter the loan amount at least 1000 BNB

opening.argument: The material presents an operational procedure with explicit contingencies rather than an unconditional promise. It acknowledges that the suggested payment may fail, says the daily fee may vary, and warns that the contract may fail below a stated amount. Those qualifications are inconsistent with presenting every outcome as certain. The tutorial also describes a transaction that depends on compilation, wallet connection, deployment, confirmation, and execution, making the result conditional on technical steps rather than automatic. A careful viewer is given reasons to verify settings and understand that execution can fail.

citations.quote: If using 0.2 BNB does not work, please try to send another 0.2 BNB (0.30 is better), as the daily fee may vary.
Avoid using very low amounts as the contract may fail below 0.15 BNB
If this program finds a profit on PancakeSwap,. It can swap.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account emphasizes promotional wording, but it overlooks the qualifications embedded in the instructions. “If” the program finds a profit, it can swap; the description expressly anticipates failure, variable fees, and minimum amounts. Those are risk disclosures about technical and financial conditions, not evidence that a return is guaranteed. The fact that a wallet and contract workflow is shown establishes an attempted procedure, not deceptive solicitation or a completed loss.

citations.quote: the daily fee may vary
the contract may fail below 0.15 BNB
If this program finds a profit on PancakeSwap,. It can swap.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The caveats concern how much to send and whether the contract runs; they do not warn that the advertised “free BNB” result is unverified or that sending funds may expose viewers to loss. The title still calls it “100% Tested,” while the instructions direct viewers to fund the contract and invoke its action. Technical contingencies therefore do not neutralize the central financial claim.

opening.argument: The video's observable structure is a software and smart-contract demonstration: it walks through Remix, file creation, compiler selection, deployment, and a contract action. The speaker explains interface choices and shows a connected development environment, which is consistent with teaching viewers how a blockchain tool operates. The description itself labels the material a “Step-by-step tutorial,” and the spoken narration repeatedly gives procedural instructions. A demonstration of code execution should not automatically be treated as certification that every possible result is genuine or guaranteed.

we're going to go. Back up to compiler
There's our new contract we just launched on PancakeSwap. Oh, no, not on PancakeSwap. We launched it on the BNB Smart Chain.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account treats the instructional format as proof of a scam, but its own evidence describes a recorded workflow, not a verified promise of results. The quoted directions concern using Remix, choosing a compiler, deploying a contract, and waiting for confirmation. Showing those operations is materially different from proving that the contract generates profit or that viewers suffered a loss. The most defensible reading is technical demonstration with an accompanying financial use case.

citations.quote: we're going to go. Back up to compiler

So we're going to wait a little bit for that to go through.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not make the subject merely technical. The tutorial is specifically framed around “FREE BNB,” tells viewers to copy supplied contract code, connect MetaMask, borrow 1000 BNB, and fund the contract. The instructional format is the delivery mechanism for the financial solicitation, and the closing narration claims an amount was made rather than merely explaining syntax.

opening.argument: At most, the material describes use of ordinary publicly available software and a blockchain transaction process. It points to Remix, a code file, compiler settings, MetaMask, and a smart-contract deployment; those are tools and operational steps, not evidence of a hidden downline, credential harvest, or guaranteed investment account. The described transfer is characterized as funding for gas or swaps, and the instructions identify a transaction confirmation before the contract action. Without establishing what the recipient contract does, who controls it, or whether any profit was actually received, the record does not establish the defining mechanism of a scam.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The evidence shows a code-driven transaction workflow, but it does not identify a fraudulent recipient, stolen credentials, downline, or guaranteed return. The opposing account concedes that the recipient, contract behavior, and actual profit are not established. Those omissions matter: a transfer used for gas or swaps can be risky, but risk alone does not prove that the content is a scam. The record supports treating this as a blockchain service or demonstration whose safety remains unverified.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract to get the gas fee for all swaps
We launched it on the BNB Smart Chain.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing details do not make the mechanism ordinary. The content promotes “free” BNB, directs viewers to copy code from an external link, requires wallet connection, specifies a 1000 BNB loan, and then instructs them to send BNB to the deployed contract. The absence of a named recipient or independently verified contract behavior is precisely why the transaction cannot be treated as an ordinary safe service. The video also depicts a contract interaction showing a 0.15 BNB transfer.
